Combines dense retrieval with multi-hop traversal over an MITRE ATT&CK-seeded knowledge graph.
Grounds generated leads in the defender’s assets and controls, producing structured outputs rather than loose IOCs.
Evaluated on public reports about well-known APTs across proprietary and open-weight models.
Hybrid retrieval and ontology grounding improve mean F1 from 0.44 to 0.85 over flat RAG; reported effectiveness is about 86.95%.
papers.selection_reason: Introduces AHLERT, a system for evidence-grounded retrieval in cybersecurity using RAG and LLMs, demonstrating a practical application of LLMs to complex information retrieval tasks.
papers.title: Evidence-Grounded Retrieval for Investigation Hunt Lead Generation from CTI Reports
papers.tldr: AHLERT generates environment-aware, actionable threat-hunting leads from CTI reports by combining hybrid evidence retrieval, knowledge-graph traversal, and ontology-grounded RAG.

papers.abstract: Large language model (LLM) benchmarks are often treated as fixed datasets with stable scores, yet their outcomes depend on configurable evaluation pipelines. We audit eight cybersecurity benchmarks across 10 proprietary, open-weight, and cybersecurity-specialized LLMs. By modeling benchmarks as measurement pipelines, we identify 15 systematic failure modes and show that a single pipeline choice can change a model's score by more than 80 percentage points and substantially alter model rankings. At the cross-benchmark level, two semantically similar task pairs rank the same models differently because of incompatible evaluation conventions. Under an evaluation harness that standardizes pipeline choices while preserving task semantics, nine of 10 models shift by at least three ranks on at least one benchmark. These results show that cybersecurity LLM benchmark scores are pipeline-dependent and motivate pipeline-aware auditing as a core requirement for reliable model evaluation.
authors: Aymene Berriche
Cathrine Shalby
Mohannad Alhanahnah
Yazan Boshmaf
bullets: Audits eight cybersecurity benchmarks across 10 proprietary, open-weight, and specialized LLMs.
Identifies 15 systematic evaluation-pipeline failure modes.
A single pipeline choice can change scores by over 80 percentage points and substantially alter rankings.
Semantically similar tasks can rank the same models differently under incompatible evaluation conventions.
Standardizing pipeline choices changes the rankings of nine of 10 models on at least one benchmark.
papers.selection_reason: Investigates the reliability of LLM evaluation pipelines, a critical methodological aspect of LLM research that impacts how models are benchmarked and compared.
papers.title: Benchmark Scores Are Pipeline-Dependent: A Reliability Audit of Cybersecurity LLM Benchmarks
papers.tldr: Cybersecurity LLM benchmark scores and rankings can change dramatically with evaluation-pipeline choices, making pipeline-aware auditing essential for reliable comparisons.

papers.abstract: Object-centric manipulation policies improve generalization by modeling object motion instead of directly predicting robot actions. However, existing methods are often limited by representations which are either too simplistic to capture interaction dynamics or too dense to learn efficiently. We observe that many rigid relational manipulation tasks are governed by short interaction phases where the relative motion between task-relevant objects is tightly constrained. Based on this observation, we propose \textsc{Foci Policy}, an interaction-centric framework that achieves a two-fold abstraction: (1) temporally, by automatically extracting compact interaction segments from demonstrations;(2) spatially, by representing skills as relative $SE(3)$ motion between task-relevant objects, yielding invariance to scene configurations and robot embodiment. Experiments on RLBench, COLOSSEUM, and real-world tasks show that \textsc{Foci Policy} achieves strong performance with substantially less training data than prior object-centric and action-centric policies. These results suggest that modeling object-object interactions provides a simple and efficient inductive bias for rigid relational manipulation. Project page: \href{https://fitz0401.github.io/foci-page/}{fitz0401.github.io/foci-page/}.
authors: Ze Fu
Pinhao Song
Yutong Hu
Renaud Detry
bullets: Targets the tradeoff between overly simplistic and overly dense representations for relational manipulation.
Automatically extracts compact interaction segments from demonstrations.
Represents skills using relative SE(3) motion between task-relevant objects, supporting scene and robot-embodiment invariance.
Evaluations on RLBench, COLOSSEUM, and real-world tasks show strong performance with substantially less training data than prior approaches.
Scope: designed for rigid relational manipulation tasks governed by constrained relative motion.
papers.selection_reason: Object-centric interaction modeling for relational manipulation directly fits robot learning and manipulation.
papers.title: FOCI Policy: Focus on Object-Centric Interactions for Relational Manipulation Policies
papers.tldr: FOCI Policy learns efficient, generalizable manipulation skills by modeling short object-object interaction phases as relative 3D motions.

papers.abstract: We present DCLP++, a local navigation frameworkthat uses footprint clearance as the geometric basis for studying relative motion features in dynamic environments. Each valid LiDAR return is mapped to its shortest Euclidean distance from the filled robot footprint before reciprocal encoding, replacing distance from the sensor with distance to the occupied body. Radial measurementsor simulated planar relative velocities provide short-horizon features without static-dynamic labels in the policy input. A preliminary study uses a rectangular robot with a speed limit of 1 m/s among 20 moving obstacles. On 100 fixed validation tasks, two selected training seeds yield mean success rates of 42% with sensor rangeand 70% with footprint clearance after 200,000 environment steps.Motion variants show mixed additional gains. These results supportthe clearance-based observation in the evaluated setting; reliable motion benefits and transfer across robots require further evaluation.
authors: Shanze Wang
Wei Zhang
bullets: Uses footprint clearance—the shortest distance from each LiDAR return to the occupied robot body—as the geometric observation basis.
Adds radial measurements or simulated planar relative velocities as short-horizon motion features without static/dynamic labels.
In a preliminary setting with a rectangular robot and 20 moving obstacles, footprint clearance reached 70% mean success versus 42% for sensor-range distance after 200,000 steps.
Motion features produced mixed additional gains.
Reliable motion benefits and transfer to other robots remain unverified.
papers.selection_reason: Local robot navigation with footprint clearance and relative motion fits learned navigation policies.
papers.title: DCLP++: Learning to Navigate with Footprint Clearance and Relative Motion
papers.tldr: DCLP++ improves local navigation in dynamic environments by encoding LiDAR relative to the robot’s footprint, substantially increasing validation success in a preliminary study.

papers.abstract: Long-form instructional videos require automatic chaptering to support browsing, navigation, and knowledge access. Recent long-context language models can perform chaptering from textualized video inputs, but they remain costly and brittle for content-dense lecture videos with long transcripts, smooth topic transitions, and detailed chapter outputs. A scalable segment-then-caption paradigm reduces this cost, but introduces two new challenges: boundary error propagation and fragmented cross-chapter context. We propose \textbf{CausalChapter}, an intervention-inspired framework for long-video chaptering that estimates prediction-level influence through lightweight masking and removal interventions. For boundary localization, our Local Dependency Shift module detects drops in predictive dependency between adjacent temporal windows; for chapter description generation, our Cross-Segment Support Selection module reranks historical contexts according to their support for the current prediction. Experiments on long-video chaptering benchmarks show that CausalChapter improves boundary localization, chapter description quality, and cross-chapter coherence.
authors: Xinran Duan
Guozhang Li
Yaoyao Zhong
Mei Wang
Lizhi Wang
Hua Huang
bullets: Targets costly and brittle chaptering of content-dense instructional videos with long transcripts and smooth topic transitions.
Addresses boundary error propagation and fragmented context in segment-then-caption systems.
Uses masking/removal interventions to estimate prediction-level influence.
Detects boundary shifts via local dependency changes and reranks historical context for chapter descriptions.
Experiments report better boundary localization, description quality, and cross-chapter coherence on long-video chaptering benchmarks.
papers.selection_reason: Long-video chaptering with causal dependency modeling directly targets video understanding.
papers.title: CausalChapter: Improving Long-Video Chaptering with Interventional Dependency Modeling
papers.tldr: CausalChapter improves scalable long-video chaptering by using lightweight intervention-based dependency modeling to localize boundaries and select useful cross-segment context.

papers.abstract: In multi-party human-robot interaction, a robot must continuously decide whom to address and what to say to participate effectively in the conversation. In real-world interactions, this is challenging because several behaviours may be plausible at the same time: a robot might continue a topic with one participant, involve another through a question, or address the whole group, with the appropriate choice depending on both whom it addresses and the interaction context. Current approaches remain limited in representing uncertainty when several behaviours are plausible and in structuring decisions into semantically meaningful intermediate steps that make robot decisions easier to interpret. Addressing these, we present HiBRIDGE, a hierarchical Bayesian neural network framework for group-robot dialogue management. Its Bayesian formulation enables uncertainty-aware prediction and robust learning from limited interaction data, while the hierarchical approach formulates behaviour selection as a structured, multi-stage decision process. We further use decision-tree surrogates to investigate whether this structure can support more interpretable explanations. Across three offline group-HRI datasets, our findings show that Bayesian formulations outperform their deterministic counterparts and several state-of-the-art baselines. Next, through an online study (N=20), we show that explanations derived from the hierarchical model are rated as more helpful for understanding robot behaviour and are preferred over those derived from the flat model. Finally, through our in-person study (N=12), we demonstrate the feasibility of HiBRIDGE for autonomous real-time group interaction, with both hierarchical and flat Bayesian variants positively perceived. Overall, HiBRIDGE combines strong predictive performance with a structured decision process that supports more interpretable explanations of robot behaviour.
authors: Massimiliano Nigro
Hatice Gunes
Micol Spitale
Fethiye Irmak Dogan
bullets: Addresses the challenge of choosing whom to address and what to say when multiple behaviours are plausible.
Uses Bayesian prediction for uncertainty awareness and learning from limited interaction data.
Structures behaviour selection as a hierarchical, multi-stage process, with decision-tree surrogates for explanations.
Outperformed deterministic variants and several baselines across three offline group-HRI datasets.
User studies found hierarchical explanations more helpful and preferred, while in-person results demonstrated feasible real-time interaction.
papers.selection_reason: Group-robot dialogue management with interpretable Bayesian modeling is an embodied interaction task.
papers.title: HiBRIDGE: A Hierarchical Bayesian Neural Network Framework for Interpretable Dialogue Management in Group-Robot Interaction
papers.tldr: HiBRIDGE uses hierarchical Bayesian modeling to help robots make uncertain, interpretable dialogue decisions in group interactions.

papers.abstract: Exploration in reinforcement learning (RL) remains a fundamental challenge. Recent goal-conditioned RL strategies (which select goals to encourage broader state coverage) have shown promising results, but none scores a goal by novelty and reachability jointly: the two signals are traded off by hand, applied in sequence, or one is neglected outright. In this paper, we introduce a reachability-aware goal-selection framework that explicitly integrates these two aspects, and that can be seamlessly incorporated into any off-policy RL algorithm. To this aim, we propose SUccessor-to-Novelty (SUN), an indicator derived from successor value functions to identify goals that are both novel and reachable. We prove that SUN recovers count-based bonuses in the limit, bounds short-horizon hitting probabilities, and provably rejects unreachable goals. We further present an adaptive goal-selection strategy that leverages these properties, and an accurate yet lightweight pseudocount to avoid the overhead of classic methods. We back up all our claims with thorough benchmarks: SUN consistently outperforms state-of-the-art methods in standard and novel environments with unreachable or hard-to-reach states, irreversible transitions, obstacles, mazes, and unbounded spaces.
authors: Wenyan Yang
Arsenii Mustafin
Dominik Baumann
Joni Pajarinen
Simone Parisi
bullets: Addresses the lack of methods jointly scoring goal novelty and reachability.
Introduces SUN, a successor-value-based indicator compatible with any off-policy RL algorithm.
Provides theoretical guarantees: count-based bonuses in the limit, bounds on short-horizon hitting probabilities, and rejection of unreachable goals.
Adds adaptive goal selection and a lightweight pseudocount to reduce the overhead of classic methods.
Benchmarks report consistent gains over state-of-the-art methods across diverse environments, including mazes, obstacles, irreversible transitions, and unbounded spaces.
papers.selection_reason: Reachability-aware RL exploration method is transferable to embodied robot learning and control.
papers.title: SUN: Reaching for Novelty in Reinforcement Learning
papers.tldr: SUN selects reinforcement-learning goals that are both novel and reachable, improving exploration across challenging environments.

papers.abstract: An action chunk can span several stages of a manipulation task, yet a label for its first step describes only the current stage. We introduce Chunk-Aligned Semantic Distillation (CASD), which derives semantic targets for entire action chunks. An offline vision--language model segments demonstrations into described stages. Their occupancy within each action chunk determines a weighted semantic target, including transitions between stages. A CASD generator learns to predict this target from the current observation, robot state, and task instruction. We then freeze the generator and train a policy conditioned on its predictions. The semantic branch runs once per policy query, without online VLM calls or reasoning-trace decoding. Teacher matching on annotated LIBERO training episodes is above chance for both single-stage and boundary-crossing chunks. We evaluate three Fast-WAM variants and a DreamZero integration across four benchmarks, including distribution shifts on LIBERO-Plus. Compared with published references, IDM+CASD reaches 98.9\% versus 98.0\% average success on LIBERO, while Uncond falls below its reference. Joint+CASD reaches 93.0\% versus 90.6\% on RoboTwin 2.0, and DreamZero+CASD reaches a 47.9\% four-category MolmoSpaces manipulation average versus 40.7\%. Performance varies across backbone integrations.
authors: Tinghe Ding
Jiahao Li
He Wang
bullets: Addresses the mismatch between first-step labels and action chunks that span multiple manipulation stages.
Uses an offline vision-language model to segment demonstrations and derive occupancy-weighted semantic targets, including stage transitions.
Trains a semantic generator from observations, robot state, and task instructions, then freezes it while training the policy.
The semantic branch runs once per policy query without online VLM calls or reasoning-trace decoding.
Improves reported averages for several integrations and benchmarks, though performance varies by backbone; teacher matching is above chance on annotated LIBERO episodes.
papers.selection_reason: Multi-stage robot manipulation with VLM-derived semantic targets fits robot learning and vision-language-action.
papers.title: CASD: Chunk-Aligned Semantic Distillation for Multi-StageRobot Manipulation
papers.tldr: CASD improves multi-stage robot manipulation by distilling stage-aware semantics for entire action chunks into a policy-conditioning signal.

papers.abstract: Egocentric 4D interaction forecasting aims to anticipate both where future interactions will occur in 3D and how the human body will move to realize them, providing an important capability for assistive robotics and human-computer interaction. Existing methods struggle to translate semantic understanding into precise continuous 3D localization and to balance motion diversity with structural consistency in pose forecasting. More fundamentally, these tasks are often modeled separately, leaving the continuous geometric and temporal correspondence between interaction locations and body motion insufficiently captured. To address these challenges, we introduce Coherent4D, a large-scale egocentric dataset for continuous 4D interaction forecasting, comprising approximately 233K samples across three domains. Each sample pairs a sequence of future 3D interaction locations with corresponding full-body poses, aligned in time and expressed in a shared coordinate system. We also provide evaluation metrics in continuous space. Building on this formulation, we propose HIGFlow, a Hand Interaction Guided Residual Flow framework that models forecasting as a cascaded where-to-how process. HIGFlow first forecasts continuous future interaction locations by combining semantic grounding with short-horizon visual dynamics, and then uses the predicted location sequence to condition a deterministic motion anchor and residual Flow Matching for diverse yet structurally consistent full-body motion forecasting. Extensive experiments across all three domains demonstrate consistent improvements over representative baselines on both location and pose forecasting, while ablations validate the contributions of the proposed components. The project page is available at https://corrineqiu.github.io/from-where-to-how/.
authors: Qiaohui Chu
Haoyu Zhang
Meng Liu
Haoxiang Shi
Dongmei Jiang
Liqiang Nie
bullets: Introduces Coherent4D, a large-scale egocentric dataset with time-aligned future 3D interaction locations and full-body poses across three domains.
Defines continuous-space evaluation for joint interaction-location and motion forecasting.
HIGFlow uses a cascaded “where-to-how” design: it predicts interaction locations, then conditions motion generation on them.
Combines semantic grounding, visual dynamics, deterministic motion anchors, and residual Flow Matching to produce diverse, structurally consistent poses.
Experiments report consistent improvements over representative baselines for both location and pose forecasting; ablations support the proposed components.
papers.selection_reason: Egocentric 4D interaction forecasting from human video directly supports embodied skill learning and video understanding.
papers.title: From Where to How: Continuous 4D Interaction Forecasting from Egocentric Video
papers.tldr: Coherent4D and HIGFlow jointly forecast where future interactions will occur and how the body will move to perform them from egocentric video.

papers.abstract: Autonomous navigation in unstructured environments requires robust scene understanding, yet Vision-Language Models (VLMs) often suffer from semantic ambiguity, where conflicting predictions can lead to dangerous failures. To address this, we present a novel pipeline for vision-based traversability estimation that explicitly models contextual uncertainty. Our approach utilizes Conceptual Anchoring to ground open-vocabulary VLM predictions onto a continuous physical traversability scale. By formulating the model's responses as a Gaussian Context Distribution (GCD), we derive both a dense traversability map and a dense uncertainty map based on the statistical properties of the distribution. Experimental validation on the real-world GOOSE dataset demonstrates that our proposed uncertainty metric effectively correlates with sources of ambiguity, such as visual artifacts and mixed terrain overlap. The method exhibits competitive performance while offering the distinct advantage of providing statistical uncertainty estimates to address semantic ambiguity, enabling safer and more reliable autonomous behavior in complex outdoor settings.
authors: Ramona Häuselmann
Mario A. V. Saucedo
Christoforos Kanellakis
George Nikolakopoulos
bullets: Addresses dangerous navigation failures caused by conflicting or ambiguous VLM predictions.
Uses Conceptual Anchoring to map open-vocabulary predictions onto a continuous physical traversability scale.
Represents VLM responses as a Gaussian Context Distribution, yielding dense traversability and uncertainty maps.
On the real-world GOOSE dataset, the uncertainty metric correlates with visual artifacts and mixed-terrain overlap.
Provides statistical uncertainty estimates with competitive performance, though the abstract does not specify quantitative results or limitations.
papers.selection_reason: VLM-driven traversability estimation with explicit uncertainty modeling for autonomous navigation; fits robot navigation and obstacle avoidance.
papers.title: Estimating Semantic Ambiguity via Gaussian Context Distributions for VLM-Driven Traversability Analysis
papers.tldr: A VLM-based traversability pipeline models semantic ambiguity with Gaussian context distributions to produce both traversability and uncertainty maps for safer outdoor navigation.

papers.abstract: Autonomous exploration on uneven terrain requires ground robots to balance exploration efficiency, coverage completeness, and terrain safety. Detailed tsrrain reasoning improves local reliability but can slow large-scale exploration, whereas coarse region guidance expands quickly in open areas but can miss narrow passages and irregular traversable boundaries. To address this challenge, this paper presents TASG-Explore, a traversability-aware sector-guided exploration framework for ground robots. The framework first performs hierarchical traversability analysis using variable-voxel ground fitting and adaptive 8-bit obstacle encoding. It then splitting cost map into sectors, incrementally updates sector clusters, extracts terrain-coupled frontier viewpoints, and maintains a dynamic topological roadmap with unknown topological hypotheses. Finally, a sector-guided planner selects region targets and inserts local viewpoints to generate efficient exploration routes. Benchmark experiments in diverse challenging environments, including caves, forests, and rugged hills, show that TASG-Explore achieves the best overall performance among six representative state-of-the-art planners. The proposed traversability analysis improves processing efficiency by 6.3 times while maintaining high accuracy, and the exploration planner improves exploration efficiency by 51% and increases coverage by up to 2.95 times in rugged hill scene. Large-scale real-world experiments further demonstrate the practical value of the proposed method.
authors: Shaocong Wang
Shiliang Shao
Ting Wang
Guangjie Han
Lianqing Liu
bullets: Addresses the trade-off between detailed terrain reasoning and fast large-scale exploration, including narrow passages and irregular traversable boundaries.
Uses variable-voxel ground fitting and adaptive 8-bit obstacle encoding for hierarchical traversability analysis.
Splits cost maps into sectors, updates sector clusters, extracts terrain-aware frontier viewpoints, and maintains a dynamic topological roadmap.
Benchmarks across caves, forests, and rugged hills report 6.3× faster traversability processing, 51% higher exploration efficiency, and up to 2.95× greater coverage in a rugged-hill scene.
Large-scale real-world experiments support the method’s practical value.
papers.selection_reason: Traversability-aware exploration planner for ground robots on uneven terrain; directly fits learned robot navigation and planning.
papers.title: TASG-Explore: Traversability-Aware Sector-Guided Exploration for Ground Robot on Uneven Terrain
papers.tldr: TASG-Explore combines hierarchical terrain analysis with sector-guided planning to improve safe, efficient, and complete ground-robot exploration on uneven terrain.

papers.abstract: Video generative models provide rich physical priors for robot learning, yet existing world-action models (WAMs) face a fundamental trade-off: synchronous video generation at control rate is latency-prohibitive, while abandoning test-time visual imagination sacrifices task success. We show that visual imagination achieves both real-time inference and superior success rates when generated asynchronously off the critical path and consumed directly in latent space. We introduce GlanceWAM, which decouples imagination from control on a single shared video DiT backbone: an asynchronous proposer glances ahead on a slow clock to imagine a single lookahead frame seconds into the future in the background, while an action head decodes action chunks at control rate (48 ms) purely in latent space without blocking. Enabled by a non-interfering attention mask that isolates video representations and staleness-robust horizon training that accommodates asynchronous lookahead aging, GlanceWAM breaks the speed-success dilemma. Trained purely on demonstrations, it attains 72.2% on the 24-task RoboCasa kitchen benchmark (vs. 67.1% for synchronous Cosmos Policy) and 99.0% on LIBERO while cutting per-chunk control latency $24\times$ relative to synchronous world-action models (48 ms on one A100). In single-arm and bimanual real-robot manipulation, it achieves higher average success than $\pi_{0.5}$ without any robot-data pretraining. Code is available at https://github.com/linhanwang/GlanceWAM.
authors: Linhan Wang, Zijian An, Mingyuan Zhang, Chen Dai, Yi Xu, Can Cui, Jiayan Wang, Zichong Yang, Yinlin Chen, Lifeng Zhou, Chang-Tien Lu
bullets: Addresses the latency–success trade-off in world-action models that use visual imagination at control time.
Uses a shared video DiT backbone with an asynchronous lookahead proposer and a control-rate action head operating without blocking.
Introduces non-interfering attention and staleness-robust horizon training for aging asynchronous predictions.
Achieves 72.2% on RoboCasa and 99.0% on LIBERO, with 48 ms control latency—24× lower than synchronous models.
Outperforms π0.5 on real single-arm and bimanual manipulation without robot-data pretraining.
papers.selection_reason: Asynchronous test-time imagination for world-action models improving robot manipulation latency and success, directly relevant to embodied AI and world models.
papers.title: GlanceWAM: Sparse Test-Time Imagination for World-Action Models
papers.tldr: GlanceWAM enables fast, effective robot control by asynchronously imagining a single future frame while decoding actions directly in latent space.

papers.abstract: Large Language Models have emerged as programming assistants. However, the efficacy of code generation is constrained by the quality of input requirements, which are frequently ambiguous, incomplete, or underspecified. While LLMs excel at one-shot code synthesis, their ability to proactively clarify intent remains underexplored, as a critical trait for robust software engineering. Existing benchmarks largely overlook this interactive bottleneck, assuming perfectly specified prompts that do not reflect the iterative nature of requirement elicitation. To bridge this gap, we introduce ClarifyCodeBench, a novel interactive benchmark for evaluating LLMs' capability in resolving requirement ambiguity. Constructed from real-world programming tasks, ClarifyCodeBench features high-quality manual annotations, including N unique ambiguity types, associated clarification questions, and corresponding ground-truth answers. Furthermore, we formalize two rigorous metrics to assess the interaction quality: Turn-discounted Key Question Rate, which penalizes inefficient questioning, and Optimal Round Adherence, which measures the precision of the elicitation process. We conduct a systematic evaluation of six state-of-the-art LLMs using ClarifyCodeBench. Our empirical results yield three critical insights: 1) Capability Decoupling: Strong code generation performance does not inherently translate to effective requirement clarification; 2) The Reasoning Paradox: While increased computational thinking enhances code correctness, it yields marginal gains in identifying ambiguities; 3) The Multi-ambiguity Ceiling: LLMs' clarification performance degrades sharply as the density of ambiguities increases, revealing a significant bottleneck in handling complex, real-world specifications. Our work underscores the necessity for future AI4SE research to transition from static synthesis to interactive elicitation.
authors: Zheng Fang, Dongming Jin, Yihong dong, Yongmin Li, Kechi Zhang, Zhi Jin, Ge Li
bullets: Introduces an interactive benchmark built from real-world programming tasks with annotated ambiguity types, clarification questions, and ground-truth answers.
Proposes Turn-discounted Key Question Rate and Optimal Round Adherence to measure questioning efficiency and elicitation precision.
Evaluates six state-of-the-art LLMs and finds that code-generation strength does not imply strong clarification ability.
More reasoning improves code correctness but provides only marginal gains in ambiguity identification.
Clarification performance drops sharply as the number of simultaneous ambiguities increases.
papers.selection_reason: Benchmark for LLMs clarifying ambiguous requirements in code generation, relevant to LLM interaction and evaluation.
papers.title: ClarifyCodeBench: Evaluating LLMs on Clarifying Ambiguous Requirements for Code Generation
papers.tldr: ClarifyCodeBench evaluates whether LLMs can interactively resolve ambiguous coding requirements rather than merely generate code from idealized prompts.

papers.abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) have shown strong capabilities in code generation, but their adherence to fine-grained user intent with multiple constraints remains a significant challenge. Our empirical analysis reveals two key observations: 1) Model performance deteriorates quickly as the number of constraints in the user intent increases, and 2) While user intent does influence the model's logits, such an influence may not be strong enough to effectively steer the decoding process. To this end, we propose Intent-Amplified Code Generation (IntentCoding), a novel decoding strategy that enhances an LLM's ability to follow user intent. IntentCoding captures the influence of user intent by masking out the intent, and applies a multi-strength ensemble mechanism to amplify the effect of user intent during generation. IntentCoding is model-agnostic, requires no additional training, and integrates seamlessly with existing decoding procedures. To enable systematic evaluation, we also construct CodeConstraints, a benchmark dataset specifically designed to test user intent compliance under varying numbers of constraints. Experiments on our constructed Constraints, as well as popular IFEvalCode, HumanEval and LiveCodeBench datasets, show that our IntentCoding model significantly improves both constraint satisfaction and functional correctness compared to standard decoding approaches. IntentCoding achieves up to 71.0% relative improvement on CodeConstraints, achieves up to 67.3% relative improvement on IFEvalCode and achieves up to 29.3% relative improvement in pass@1 on HumanEval and LiveCodeBench compared with greedy decoding.
authors: Zheng Fang, Yihong Dong, Lili Mou, Dongming Jin, Zhi Jin, Ge Li
bullets: Performance declines as user requests contain more constraints, and intent signals may be too weak to steer decoding effectively.
IntentCoding masks the user intent to estimate its influence, then uses a multi-strength ensemble to amplify that influence during generation.
The method is model-agnostic, training-free, and compatible with existing decoding procedures.
The authors introduce CodeConstraints, a benchmark for evaluating compliance with varying numbers of coding constraints.
Experiments report improvements in constraint satisfaction and functional correctness across CodeConstraints, IFEvalCode, HumanEval, and LiveCodeBench.
papers.selection_reason: Decoding strategy for LLMs to follow complex user intent in code generation, relevant to LLM instruction following.
papers.title: IntentCoding: Amplifying User Intent in Code Generation
papers.tldr: IntentCoding improves LLM code generation by amplifying user-intent signals during decoding, leading to better constraint adherence and functional correctness without additional training.
